conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been having really bad nausea and vomiting for weeks. It’s gotten worse, and I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re on peritoneal dialysis for your kidney disease, correct? Any changes in that routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m on PD. I haven’t changed the schedule, but I’ve been feeling more bloated and my stomach just isn’t moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with your history of gastroparesis. We’re going to run some tests to make sure nothing else is going on. We’ve ordered a CT scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I was also having diarrhea before I came in. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes with gastroparesis, bowel patterns get irregular. We tested your stool and it came back negative for C. diff, so it’s likely not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. Your blood pressure dropped earlier, and you were a bit confused. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I just remember feeling weak and dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low blood sugar—down to 20. That can cause confusion. We gave you glucose and fluids, and you improved quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh wow. I didn’t realize it was that low. My diabetes has been hard to manage lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with gastroparesis, it’s tough to time insulin with food that’s not moving through predictably. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I’ve been scared to eat much at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on small sips and see how you tolerate it. We also gave you some erythromycin to help your stomach empty better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve adjusted the dose for your kidney function. It’s short-term to help get things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back. No signs of infection or blockage. Your dialysis catheter is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s just my gastroparesis acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the diarrhea likely contributed to your low blood pressure. We’re continuing IV fluids and monitoring your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a little better today. Less nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll try advancing your diet slowly. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but manageable. I’ve been using the Zofran before meals like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that available for you. Also, your blood cultures and peritoneal fluid came back clean—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped them yesterday since there’s no sign of infection. Your improvement supports that decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray and another abdominal X-ray to check your catheter. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any reason to worry about pneumonia or fluid in my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lungs look clear. No signs of fluid or infection. Your blood pressure has been stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried when I got so confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think that was due to the low blood sugar and dehydration. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my anemia? My hemoglobin was low last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s still a bit low, but that’s expected with kidney disease. We’ll monitor it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a peritoneal irrigation yesterday to make sure there was no buildup causing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was precautionary. No signs of infection, but it helps clear any debris. You’re tolerating food better now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had some broth and toast this morning. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep building up slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low earlier, so we’re giving you supplements. It’s important with your diuretics and dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize I was low. Any symptoms I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Muscle cramps or weakness. We’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my insulin—what’s the plan there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your long-acting insulin because your morning sugars were too low. We’ll send you home with a new schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been waking up shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most of your usual ones. We’re continuing domperidone and lubiprostone. We stopped the erythromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tizanidine? I’ve been feeling groggy in the mornings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve lowered it from 12mg to 2mg at night. It wasn’t clearing well with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That explains it. I’ll be more alert during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea worsens, try a liquid diet for a few days. Avoid constipation—it makes gastroparesis worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow the new insulin plan. Check your potassium in a few days—we’ve ordered the lab test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your PCP, GI, and endocrinology. We’re setting up a gastroparesis specialist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Take it slow, stick to the meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. A bit tired, but no nausea or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable. Blood pressure 149/84, heart rate 89. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—avoid driving while taking lorazepam. It can add to drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, your husband is listed as your contact. He can help monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll be here soon to pick me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I feel safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what matters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.
